name: Doramad radioactive toothpaste

card.summary: A thorium-containing German toothpaste sold from the 1920s that was promoted for whiter teeth and healthier gums.
card.note: Historical product; radioactive ingredient, no longer sold.

quick.overview:
Doramad was a toothpaste made by Auergesellschaft of Berlin from the 1920s through World War II, containing small amounts of thorium from monazite sand. The maker promised whiter teeth and stronger gums.

It is a historical example of radioactivity marketed as a beauty ingredient. It is not available today.
quick.how: It was used like any toothpaste. The packaging advertised 'special biological healing effects by radium rays', though thorium was the actual element.
quick.risks: Ionizing radiation was not understood to be hazardous when it was sold. Modern readers treat it as a cautionary example.

lead: Doramad was a slightly radioactive toothpaste made by Auergesellschaft, Berlin, from the 1920s through WWII, by-product of the firm's thorium work for gas lantern mantles.[1]
The company claimed radioactivity strengthened gums and teeth, killed germs, improved circulation and added 'life force', and promised whiter teeth.[1]

Samuel Goudsmit's 1947 Time article recounted that Allied agents who suspected seized thorium was for a bomb program learned it was for toothpaste.[1] A 1950 Dermatologica case report concerned thorium X (doramad) applied to a pigmented nevus.[2]

angle.text: It was sold for whiter teeth and healthier gums; those were the maker's claims.

paras: Whether production continued after the war is unknown.[1]
A 1950 Dermatologica report described clearing of a pigmented nevus after a single application of Doramad (thorium X); it concerned skin, not teeth.[2]

timeline.event: Goudsmit's Time article on the toothpaste thorium.[1]

refs.title: Noticeable clearing up of a pigmented nevus on the lower leg following single application of doramad (thorium X)
